niches.title: Health leadership and governance
niches.description: Explore how health organisations set direction, make decisions and remain accountable to the people they serve.
practicalApplications: Mapping who makes decisions about a local health service and who can hold those decision-makers accountable.
Considering how community voices can inform service priorities.

skills.title: Stakeholder mapping
skills.explanation: Identify who decides, advises and is affected by a service change.

skills.title: Clear policy communication
skills.explanation: Explain a service priority or accountability question in clear language.

skills.title: Comparing accountability arrangements
skills.explanation: Compare where responsibilities sit and how concerns can be raised.

activity.title: Map a service decision
activity.objective: Connect a governance concept to a concrete decision and the people affected.
instructions: Choose a hypothetical decision, such as changing a clinic’s opening hours.
List five stakeholders and identify who decides, who advises and who is affected.
Sketch a simple decision map and propose one way patients could give feedback.
activity.expectedOutput: A one-page stakeholder map with a short explanation of one accountability gap.
activity.reflection: Which stakeholder voice is missing, and what would you need to check before changing the decision process?

niches.nextStep: Read the linked WHO governance overview, then revise your map with one question about participation or accountability.

illustrativePathways.explanation: A subject domain for further exploration. Check actual programme content and entry requirements with the institution; no specific programme is endorsed.

illustrativePathways.title: Exploring health programme coordination or policy implementation work
illustrativePathways.explanation: A professional domain to learn about, not a vacancy, credential or guaranteed outcome. Responsibilities and eligibility depend on the organisation and setting.

overview: Leadership and governance offers a way to examine who sets service priorities, how responsibilities are shared, and how decisions are explained to the public. You might be drawn to the organisational questions behind a service rather than only its clinical work.

For exploration, separate setting a direction from the rules and accountability arrangements that guide decisions. A hypothetical clinic decision can help you ask whose views are represented, who has authority, and how people can raise concerns. This is draft educational framing, not a description of one country’s system.

relatedNiches.explanation: Decisions about service priorities connect governance to how budgets are allocated and explained. Explore financing to ask how those decisions shape the use of funds.
Organisational responsibilities and leadership decisions connect to how health workers are deployed and supported. Explore workforce questions to see a different side of service management.

niches.nextStepOutcome: An annotated stakeholder map and one participation or accountability question.

niches.title: Health financing
niches.description: Explore how money is raised, pooled and used to pay for health services, and how these arrangements relate to access and financial protection.
practicalApplications: Comparing how a tax-funded scheme and a health insurance arrangement collect funds and pay providers.

Exploring risk pooling: sharing financial risk across a group rather than leaving each person to bear their own healthcare costs. Health insurance can be one pooling arrangement; pooling is broader than insurance. These connections require source review.

skills.title: Drawing financing flows
skills.explanation: Separate revenue collection, a shared pool and payments to providers in a diagram.

skills.title: Comparing policy trade-offs
skills.explanation: Compare inclusion and out-of-pocket costs without assuming one arrangement suits every setting.

skills.title: Interpreting basic expenditure information
skills.explanation: Read expenditure figures with attention to what they measure and what they leave out.

activity.title: Follow the money
activity.objective: Distinguish collection, pooling and purchasing in two hypothetical arrangements.
instructions: Draw a flow for a hypothetical tax-funded service: people and taxes, a pooled public budget, then payments to providers.
Draw a second flow for a hypothetical insurance scheme: member contributions, an insurance pool, then payments to providers.
Write two questions about who is included and what costs people still pay. Do not calculate premiums or recommend an insurance product.
activity.expectedOutput: Two labelled financing-flow diagrams and two questions about coverage or financial protection.
activity.reflection: Who might be outside each hypothetical pool, and what information would you need before comparing financial protection?

niches.nextStep: Check the WHO financing overview for collection, pooling and purchasing, then annotate one limitation of each hypothetical diagram.

illustrativePathways.title: Further study in health economics or health financing policy
illustrativePathways.explanation: A subject domain for further exploration. Check actual programme content and entry requirements with the institution; no specific programme is endorsed.

illustrativePathways.title: Exploring health financing analysis, insurance policy or programme budgeting domains
illustrativePathways.explanation: A professional domain to learn about, not a vacancy, credential or guaranteed outcome. Responsibilities and eligibility depend on the organisation and setting.

overview: Health financing brings together questions about raising funds, sharing financial risk and paying for services. An interest in access or affordability can lead to exploring these arrangements and the different groups they include.

Health insurance can be one arrangement for pooling resources, but pooling is broader than insurance. Exploring a hypothetical public budget alongside a hypothetical insurance pool can help distinguish collection, pooling and purchasing. This draft framing needs verification against the proposed WHO reference before authoritative use.

relatedNiches.explanation: Financing choices raise questions about who has authority over funds and who is accountable for spending. Explore governance to examine those decision arrangements.
Funding arrangements and workforce planning meet when services consider staffing resources. Explore workforce distribution without assuming that funding alone explains staffing gaps.

niches.nextStepOutcome: Two annotated diagrams, each with one clearly stated limitation.

niches.title: Health workforce
niches.description: Explore how health workers are educated, deployed, supported and retained to meet population needs.
practicalApplications: Considering why a district may have enough workers overall but unequal distribution between facilities.
Exploring how working conditions and support might affect retention in underserved areas.

skills.title: Reading workforce indicators
skills.explanation: Interpret staffing counts alongside workload, skill mix and population needs.

skills.title: Needs and capacity mapping
skills.explanation: Map available capacity and identify what information is missing before drawing conclusions.

skills.title: Comparing workforce policy options
skills.explanation: Compare recruitment, support or retention options with explicit contextual assumptions.

activity.title: Explore a staffing gap
activity.objective: Connect workforce distribution to access using a small fictional scenario.
instructions: Imagine two equally populated districts with four clinics each. District A has 40 health workers; district B has 16.
Calculate workers per clinic as a simple comparison. State that equal populations and clinic counts do not imply equal health needs.
List two missing pieces of information and propose one question about recruitment, deployment or retention.
activity.expectedOutput: A short comparison with two limitations and one workforce planning question.
activity.reflection: What does the workers-per-clinic comparison leave out, and how could that change your interpretation?

niches.nextStep: Read the WHO workforce overview, then add one consideration about education, distribution or retention to your scenario.

illustrativePathways.title: Further study in health workforce planning or health services research
illustrativePathways.explanation: A subject domain for further exploration. Check actual programme content and entry requirements with the institution; no specific programme is endorsed.

illustrativePathways.title: Exploring workforce analysis, training coordination or health service management domains
illustrativePathways.explanation: A professional domain to learn about, not a vacancy, credential or guaranteed outcome. Responsibilities and eligibility depend on the organisation and setting.

overview: Health workforce exploration focuses on the people who make health services possible: their education, roles, distribution, working conditions and support. An interest in unequal service capacity may lead you to ask how workforce decisions are made.

A simple worker count does not explain the full picture. Skills, workload, geography and population needs can change what a staffing comparison means. Treat a fictional staffing scenario as a starting point for questions rather than a staffing recommendation.

relatedNiches.explanation: Workforce decisions connect to organisational roles, participation and accountability. Explore governance to ask who shapes deployment or retention decisions.

Questions about workforce resources can connect to service budgets and payment arrangements. Explore financing to examine one part of the resource picture, without treating it as the sole explanation.

niches.nextStepOutcome: A revised staffing comparison with one education, distribution or retention consideration.

concepts.title: Accountability
concepts.interestPrompt: Who makes decisions, and how are they held accountable?

connections.explanation: An interest in accountability connects to how health organisations assign responsibility and explain decisions.

concepts.title: Community participation
concepts.interestPrompt: How can communities help shape a service?

connections.explanation: An interest in participation connects to stakeholder engagement and whose views inform service priorities.

concepts.title: Risk pooling and insurance
concepts.interestPrompt: How can people share the financial risk of healthcare?

connections.explanation: An interest in risk sharing connects to pooled financing arrangements, including health insurance where applicable. Insurance and pooling are not interchangeable terms.

concepts.title: Financial protection
concepts.interestPrompt: What happens when healthcare costs are hard to afford?

connections.explanation: An interest in affordability connects to how financing arrangements affect what people pay when using care.

concepts.title: Workforce distribution
concepts.interestPrompt: Why are health workers unevenly distributed?

connections.explanation: An interest in service capacity connects to workforce planning and the distribution of health workers.

concepts.title: Supporting and retaining workers
concepts.interestPrompt: What helps health workers stay and do their work well?

connections.explanation: An interest in working conditions connects to how health services support and retain their workforce.
